clue.text: Physio service, 75 cents?

indicators.note: seventy-five cents is three quarters of a hundred, so keep three of the four letters of the currency

parts.note: a Mass is a church service
three of the four letters of EURO, as 75 cents is three quarters of a euro

explanation.surface: A price list for physiotherapy, with some treatment costing just seventy-five cents.
explanation.walkthrough: The 75 cents is not a price but an instruction: a euro is 100 cents, so take three quarters of its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A masseur gives massage, the hands-on body treatment a physiotherapist also offers, so the two roles are loosely equivalent.

clue.text: Big fish mostly produce nothing

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: to produce is to make
zero, nothing, looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: A big fish that mostly yields nothing: an angler's disappointing catch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Produce' reads as a noun, farm goods, but it is the verb to make.
explanation.definitionFit: The mako is a large, fast shark of warm oceans, prized by sport anglers.

clue.text: Something carried, by girls at Cheltenham?

indicators.note: read as held by, the words that follow contain and carry the answer within them

parts.note: run the letters together across the word breaks

explanation.surface: Something carried by the pupils of Cheltenham Ladies' College, a famous English girls' boarding school.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer runs across girlS AT CHELtenham; the comma separates the definition, but the whole clue also describes a schoolgirl's bag.
explanation.definitionFit: A satchel is a school bag worn over the shoulder, so it is literally an item that pupils carry around.

clue.text: Cast starts to extemporise in a TV show

indicators.note: to cast metal is to pour and remould it, so the letters take a new shape
the starts of words are their opening letters, so only initials are kept

parts.note: the initial letters of the two words
taken as written

explanation.surface: A television cast is told to start improvising on air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cast' looks like the actors, but it is the anagram signal; 'a TV show' reads as one phrase, yet only 'show' defines and 'a TV' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Evita is the Lloyd Webber and Rice stage musical about Eva Perón, a famous theatre production.

clue.text: Dictator's sat on ass, saving carbon, making traffic slower

indicators.note: a dictator here is someone dictating, speaking words for another to write down, so we hear rather than read

parts.note: to sit on a horse is to ride it, past tense rode, which is pronounced the same as a street

indicators.note: saving can mean except, so that element is left out

parts.note: an ass and a chump are both fools
C is the chemical symbol for carbon

explanation.surface: A tyrant rides a donkey through town, holding up all the traffic behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dictator' suggests a tyrant but means one who dictates aloud; the ass is not the donkey being sat on but a fool, CHUMP, which then loses C.
explanation.definitionFit: A road hump is a raised ridge across a street, built precisely to force vehicles to reduce speed; the definition is descriptive rather than a synonym.

clue.text: Le Petomane's act reportedly gut-related?

indicators.note: what is reported is heard spoken, so the sound matters, not the spelling

parts.note: Le Pétomane was a French music-hall performer who farted on stage, so his act was a trick with wind

explanation.surface: A comment on the famous Parisian flatulist, whose act clearly relied on his intestines.
explanation.walkthrough: Le Pétomane (Joseph Pujol) was a professional farter at the Moulin Rouge; his routine was a gas trick, which said together sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Gastric means relating to the stomach, part of the digestive tract, which is what gut-related loosely covers.

clue.text: Hooter raised after game continues

parts.note: Go is a Japanese board game

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting something up makes it read from bottom to top

parts.note: hooter is slang for the nose

explanation.surface: A siren or horn sounds after the match, and play carries on regardless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' puts the reversed hooter behind the game. Hooter is informal British slang for a nose.
explanation.definitionFit: To go on is a common phrasal verb meaning to keep going or proceed without stopping.

clue.text: Concession on that man's tax for dodgy reason

parts.note: a sop is a small concession made to pacify someone
belonging to him
to tax someone's patience is to try it

explanation.surface: A tax break granted to one man, with suspect justification behind it.
explanation.walkthrough: Tax is not a levy but a verb: to tax is to strain or try.
explanation.definitionFit: Sophistry is clever but deceptive argument, reasoning that sounds plausible yet is fallacious, hence dodgy.

clue.text: Soldiers claim to protect lives in later edition

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround it, so one element goes around another

parts.note: the Royal Engineers, a British army corps
to sue is to make a legal claim
is alive, exists

explanation.surface: Troops make a legal claim to protect lives, recorded in a later printing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lives' looks like the plural of life, but it is the verb: he lives, that is, he is.
explanation.definitionFit: A reissue is a book or record published again after its first release, so a subsequent printing.

clue.text: Shackles on a donkey drag continuously

parts.note: shackles are chains
moke is British slang for a donkey

explanation.surface: A donkey in shackles drags its load along without a break.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drag' suggests hauling, but it is a pull on a cigarette.
explanation.definitionFit: To chain-smoke is to light one cigarette after another, taking puffs without pause.

clue.text: Sea creature, according to Spooner a funny sponge?

indicators.note: Spooner was famed for swapping the opening sounds of words, so initial sounds trade places

parts.note: funny is witty and a sponge is a cake; witty cake with its first sounds swapped

explanation.surface: A funny sponge from the sea, in the words of the famously tongue-tied Reverend Spooner.
explanation.walkthrough: Sponge looks like the sea animal but is a sponge cake; swap the W and K of witty cake.
explanation.definitionFit: The kittiwake is a small gull that lives far out on the ocean, so a seabird counts as a marine creature.

clue.text: Italy's first secretary bites lip

indicators.note: whatever bites takes something between its jaws, so one piece closes around another

parts.note: PA is a personal assistant
the lip of a cup is its rim

explanation.surface: Italy's first female secretary gets a bite on the lip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Italy's first' looks like the letter I, but it is the definition: the Italian word for first.
explanation.definitionFit: Prima is the feminine Italian for first, familiar from prima donna and prima ballerina.

clue.text: Over-involved head briefly beat popular boy

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the final letter is removed

parts.note: taken as written
a throb is a beat, as of the heart
what is in is fashionable
a son is a boy

explanation.surface: A headteacher, far too involved, quickly strikes a well-liked pupil.
explanation.walkthrough: HEAD loses its D. W. Heath Robinson was a British cartoonist who drew absurdly elaborate contraptions for simple tasks.
explanation.definitionFit: Heath-Robinson describes a device that is ridiculously complicated for its purpose, which is what over-involved means here.

clue.text: Cut your tree after serious complaint

indicators.note: after means coming behind, so the word before it is placed second in the answer

parts.note: TB, tuberculosis, is a serious disease
one's is the impersonal form of your
teak is a hardwood tree

explanation.surface: A tree surgeon's instruction: cut down your tree after a nasty illness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After' places the tree behind the rest. 'Your' as in 'one's' is the general-person pronoun.
explanation.definitionFit: A T-bone steak is a particular cut of beef, taken from the short loin with a T-shaped bone.

clue.text: Golf, say, with out of place AMG label

indicators.note: letters that are out of place are not in their proper order and need rearranging

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A Volkswagen Golf fitted with a Mercedes-AMG badge that doesn't belong on it.
explanation.walkthrough: Golf reads as the car model next to AMG, the Mercedes performance brand, but it is the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: Golf is played by striking a small ball, so it is one example of a sport using a ball.

clue.text: Thorough checks an advantage when using Tinder?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: careful inspections, having a proper look
second meaning: attractiveness, which helps on a dating app where profiles are judged by photos

explanation.walkthrough: Tinder is a dating app on which users swipe according to photographs, so appearance counts.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is both a careful inspection in the plural and a noun for handsome or pretty appearance.

clue.text: Get from the internet 'vapour' having entered 'term for vapour'

indicators.note: one thing having something entered into it now holds it inside

parts.note: steam is water vapour

indicators.note: a term is an end or limit, so only the final letter is taken

parts.note: the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A playful definition of vaping jargon: what you call one sort of vapour inside another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Term for vapour' reads as 'a word meaning vapour', but term means end: the last letter of vapour goes into STEAM.
explanation.definitionFit: To stream audio or video is to receive and play it over the internet as it downloads.

clue.text: Surgeon reformed by a new boss

indicators.note: something reformed has been made over into a different shape, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A hospital surgeon changes their ways under a new head of department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'By' only links; 'reformed' looks like the surgeon mending their ways but signals the rearrangement.
explanation.definitionFit: Sawbones is an old humorous slang name for a doctor, especially one who amputates limbs.

clue.text: Dram nearly £25 in Japan

indicators.note: nearly means not quite complete, so the final letter goes

parts.note: a nip is a small drink of spirits
a pony is British slang for twenty-five pounds

explanation.surface: A whisky costs almost twenty-five pounds in Tokyo.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' only links the wordplay to the definition. PONY loses its Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Nippon is the Japanese people's own name for their country, used in English as an alternative.

clue.text: Will checking hold up a teacher, initially, during lesson?

indicators.note: one thing happening during another sits inside it

parts.note: PE is physical education, a school lesson
to hold up a bank is to rob it
taken as written

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter only of the word before it

parts.note: the opening letter

explanation.surface: A student asks whether a teacher will be mugged in the middle of class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Will' looks like the future tense but is the legal document, and PE (physical education) is the usual crossword lesson.
explanation.definitionFit: Probate is the legal process of proving that a deceased person's testament is valid, so it is the checking of it.

clue.text: Decline sandwiches with thanks in simple speech

indicators.note: bread sandwiches a filling by lying on either side of it

parts.note: to balk is to refuse or decline
by can mean with or beside
ta is informal British for thanks

explanation.surface: Someone politely turns down the offer of sandwiches, saying thanks in plain words.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sandwiches' looks like food but means holds between. Ta is everyday British slang for thank you.
explanation.definitionFit: Baby talk is the simplified language adults use to toddlers or that infants produce, so it is simple speech.

clue.text: Bitter golfer takes five, three taken by most

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside yourself

parts.note: bitter is a type of British beer
Ernie Els is a South African golfer
V is the Roman numeral for five

explanation.surface: A disgruntled golfer takes a five on a hole where most players manage three.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf scores are false: A levels are English school-leaving exams, most students taking three subjects.
explanation.definitionFit: Students applying to university in England usually sit three of these advanced qualifications, so the definition describes them.

clue.text: Ticket for every child except the last

indicators.note: except the last means leaving off the final letter

parts.note: per means for each
a mite is a small child

explanation.surface: A family buys admission for every child except the youngest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The last' looks like the last child, but it is the last letter of MITE, a small child.
explanation.definitionFit: A permit is a document granting entry or permission, just as a ticket authorises admission.

clue.text: One of our members ought to fancy Dr Beale

parts.note: should means ought to

indicators.note: fancy means elaborate or imaginative, so the letters are dressed up into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A club member ought to fall for Dr Beale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Our members' sounds like a club, but the members are our body parts; fancy is British for being attracted to someone, here the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The shoulder blade is a bone forming part of the human body, so it is one of our physical parts, loosely a member.

clue.text: Dad mounted pictures out of consideration

indicators.note: in a down clue, whatever is mounted climbs upward, so it reads bottom to top

parts.note: pa is an informal word for father
pictures are art

explanation.surface: Father framed and hung the pictures without really thinking about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mounted' suggests framing pictures, but it turns the father upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: As in 'joking apart', the word means set aside or left out, not taken into account.

clue.text: Fishy end for puzzle, see

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is kept

parts.note: the last letter of the word
a see is a bishop's diocese; Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire

explanation.surface: A crossword with a suspicious ending: look and see for yourself.
explanation.walkthrough: 'See' looks like an instruction to look, but it is a bishop's seat, the usual crossword route to ELY.
explanation.definitionFit: Eely means like an eel, slippery and wriggling, so it is fishy in both a literal and figurative sense.

clue.text: English singer given zero help with the lyrics

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for English
one who sings to the police is an informer, a rat
zero looks like the letter O

explanation.surface: An English vocalist is offered no assistance with learning the words of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: The singer is not a vocalist but a grass: to sing is slang for informing on criminals.
explanation.definitionFit: Erato is the Greek Muse of lyric and love poetry, a source of inspiration for writing verse.

clue.text: Element of graphic art seen all over the place

parts.note: manga is Japanese comic-book art

indicators.note: something all over the place is scattered and disordered, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A feature of graphic design that turns up everywhere you look.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Element of graphic art' reads as a design feature, but 'Element' alone is the definition and 'graphic art' is the Japanese comic form.
explanation.definitionFit: Manganese is a metallic chemical element with atomic number 25, used in steelmaking.

clue.text: Parliament showing some weakness: Etonians

indicators.note: showing only some of the words means part of their run of letters is displayed

parts.note: run the letters together across the word break

explanation.surface: A dig at a parliament dominated by old boys of Eton, England's most famous private school.
explanation.walkthrough: Old Etonians are famously common in the British parliament, but the parliament is Israel's, running across weaKNESS ETonians.
explanation.definitionFit: The Knesset is Israel's national legislature, the country's single-chamber parliament in Jerusalem.

clue.text: Comply with authority, with fist shaken internally

indicators.note: internally means on the inside, so one part is placed within another

parts.note: to have the say is to have authority

indicators.note: something shaken is jolted about, so its letters fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone obeys the authorities while shaking their fist in private.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'with' belongs to the definition, 'Comply with'; the second is only a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To satisfy a requirement or condition is to meet or fulfil it, which is complying with it.
